# S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models

Kaixiang Wang    Junjie Li    Zhaojiacheng Zhou    Jiong Lou    Jie Li

###### Abstract

Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM
agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost,
yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter
execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1
interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token
decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit
override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored
to S1’s contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo
perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce
_evidence competition_ with original task evidence while preserving fact
invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback
search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling
verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves
relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four
benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99% mean ASR and
57.47% high-confidence ASR on jev-1.14, and causes up to 24.00% E2E
agent violations.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly solve complex, multi-step
tasks across web navigation [Yao et al. (2022)](#bib.bib29), software
workflows [Jimenez et al. (2024)](#bib.bib30), and customer service [Yao
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib36). By combining open-ended reasoning with
external tool use [Schick et al. (2023)](#bib.bib31) and environment
interaction, modern agent systems can autonomously break down user
goals, coordinate specialized tools [Shen et al. (2023)](#bib.bib32),
and complete long-horizon workflows.

However, calling a large autoregressive System-2 (S2) model at every
control step brings high latency and token cost [Leviathan et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib33); [Lin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12). To cut this
overhead, recent systems assign routine decisions to fast, typed
System-1 (S1) models like Jev [TypeSafe AI (2026)](#bib.bib26),
Kev [Palmer (2026)](#bib.bib27), and Laya [ConvAI Innovations
(2026)](#bib.bib28), mapping state $`S`$, rules $`R`$, and options
$`\mathcal{O}`$ directly to a typed choice. Yet placing S1 on the
control path creates a clear vulnerability: a wrong S1 choice can
misroute downstream S2 tool calls and cause overall system failure.

![Refer to caption](2611.16937v1/problem.png)

Figure 1: S1 VS. S2 Attack.

Unlike autoregressive S2 models that generate text token by token (Fig.
 [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
(a)), S1 models score predefined options or thresholds in one forward
pass without output decoding, often applying a confidence gate before
execution (Fig.
 [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
(b)). Flipping an S1 node therefore requires shifting competitive scores
across both decision and confidence boundaries, rather than steering
open-ended text continuation. As a result, generative jailbreaks [Wei et
al. (2023)](#bib.bib35); [Zou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib20); [Liu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib21) and indirect prompt injections [Greshake et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib24); [Wallace et al. (2024)](#bib.bib34) face a clear
mismatch: S1 interfaces leave no multi-token continuation to hijack and
evaluate fixed options under $`R`$ instead of following imperative
commands. Recent studies on typed S1 models explore static injection
templates [Wu and Lim (2026)](#bib.bib3) or iterative context and suffix
search such as JevOut [Xu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2) and FlipJev [Liu et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib4). However, generic overrides and task-irrelevant
text often struggle to overturn high-margin predictions, while iterative
feedback search requires repeated per-instance queries that may be
impractical for transient decision nodes in live agents. How to
effectively manipulate unseen S1 decision contracts without relying on
iterative, instance-specific feedback remains an open challenge.

Investigating this gap, we observe that because S1 systems score state
inputs competitively against $`(R,\mathcal{O})`$, untrusted text can
flip decisions without explicit commands by inducing _evidence
competition_ with original task evidence. Motivated by this finding, we
propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving attack framework for auditing typed S1
decision models. First, given a contract $`(S,R,\mathcal{O})`$, S1-Evo
shapes command-free perturbations inside the untrusted field via
contract-aware evidence channels, weakening alignment with the
ground-truth option or anchoring a target option while preserving the
original input verbatim. Next, offline on disjoint seed tasks, feedback
search moves from broad operator probing to margin-guided refinement
using returned probabilities or scores, accepting a flip only after
independent re-verification. Finally, S1-Evo distills these verified
flips into a frozen, structure-indexed experience library and retrieves
matched patterns to construct perturbations for unseen tasks.

We evaluate S1-Evo across four benchmarks. On jev-1.14, which reaches
71.99% mean ASR and 57.47% high-confidence ASR while cutting attacker
LLM token usage by 32.10%–62.26% compared with iterative LLM baselines.
The model comparison further covers jev-1.13 and kev-4B, alongside the
generative Qwen-3.8-flash reference. Across two dual-system S1/S2 agent
workflows and two inference-time mitigations, perturbing tool outputs
and authorization notes causes up to 24.00% end-to-end violations.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- •
  We formulate the threat model for typed S1 decision contracts under
  untrusted inputs and show how supplementary evidence competition flips
  decisions across confidence gates.
- •
  We propose S1-Evo, an attack framework that combines contract-aware
  evidence channels with offline feedback search, retrieving from a
  structure-indexed experience library to construct perturbations for
  unseen tasks.
- •
  We evaluate S1-Evo across four node-level benchmarks, two dual-system
  S1/S2 agents, and two defenses, measuring both node-level
  vulnerability and system impact.

## 2 Related Work

#### S1 Decision Models.

Modern LLM systems increasingly decouple fast control-flow decisions
from open-ended text generation (e.g., [Lin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12)).
Existing pipelines enforce structured outputs via grammar-constrained
decoding [Geng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib13); [Willard and Louf
(2023)](#bib.bib14), train query routers such as RouteLLM to select
models [Chen et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib15); [Ong et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib16), or deploy fixed-taxonomy safety classifiers like
Llama Guard [Rebedea et al. (2023)](#bib.bib17); [Inan et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib18). Rather than constraining autoregressive decoding or
training task-fixed classifiers, recent typed S1 models—including Jev,
Kev, and Laya, expose a general decision interface that maps dynamic
natural-language contracts $`(S,R,\mathcal{O})`$ directly to
categorical, boolean, or scalar outputs without token-by-token output
decoding.

#### Adversarial Attacks on LLMs and Agents.

Extensive work studies attacks on generative LLMs and agentic
workflows [Mazeika et al. (2024)](#bib.bib19), including token
optimization like GCG [Zou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib20), black-box search
like AutoDAN [Liu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21); [Mehrotra et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib22), persuasive framing [Zeng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib23), and indirect prompt injection or memory poisoning
such as AgentPoison [Greshake et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24); [Chen et al.
(2024b)](#bib.bib25). However, these methods target open-ended
continuation or imperative instruction following rather than competitive
option scoring. Recent studies probe typed S1 models via prompt
injection in Decision Hijacking [Wu and Lim (2026)](#bib.bib3), neutral
background context in JevOut [Xu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2), universal
suffixes in FlipJev [Liu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4), and robustness
benchmarks in DecisionRobust [Lan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1), yet remain
limited to isolated node flips via imperative templates, task-irrelevant
context, or generic suffixes.

Moving beyond static overrides and online per-instance probing—which is
infeasible against transient S1 nodes in live agents—S1-Evo shifts
feedback search offline onto seed tasks, distilling verified flips into
a structure-indexed library to construct contract-aware perturbations in
a single pass.

## 3 System Model

In this section we will introduce the decision model and our threat
model.

### 3.1 System 1 Decision Model

In agent workflows, a System 1 (S1) decision model $`f`$ acts as a fast
node for tool routing, filtering, or authorization. While $`f`$ may use
a causal or bidirectional backbone, it avoids token-by-token generation
at inference time, mapping inputs directly to a predefined decision
space in one forward pass. Each call takes a state $`S`$, developer
rules $`R`$, and candidate space $`\mathcal{O}`$. It returns a
generalized decision output $`P`$—option probabilities for Choice, a
scalar for Score, or a binary label for Noul—and optionally an
independent confidence estimate $`C`$. The host application applies an
interpretation rule $`\pi`$ (e.g., $`\arg\max`$ or thresholding) to
$`P`$ to obtain the node decision $`\hat{y}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       (P,C)=f(S,R,\mathcal{O}),\qquad\hat{y}=\pi(P)
       ```                                            |     | (1) |

If $`C`$ is available and falls below a threshold
$`\tau_{\mathrm{conf}}`$, the decision is escalated for review rather
than executed directly.

### 3.2 Threat Model

We consider a setting where state $`S`$ mixes trusted data with
untrusted external inputs. Before the attack, the ground-truth decision
$`y^{*}`$ is independently determined from trusted facts and rules
$`R`$, remaining fixed throughout evaluation.

Attacker Capability. The attacker cannot modify $`R`$, $`\mathcal{O}`$,
or trusted fields in $`S`$, controlling only an untrusted field
$`x\in\mathrm{Ext}(S)`$ (e.g., a ticket, note, or tool output). Without
altering $`x`$, the attacker prepends or appends a misleading segment
$`\delta`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
x^{\prime}=\phi(x,\delta)\in\{\delta\|x,\;x\|\delta\},\quad\text{s.t.}\quad V(x,x^{\prime})=\mathrm{True}
``` |  | (2) |

Here, $`V(x,x^{\prime})`$ specifies validity constraints covering the
edit surface, length limits, verbatim preservation of the original
input, and ground-truth label preservation. While the syntactic
constraints can be checked programmatically, semantic label preservation
is assessed empirically through the audit in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Semantic Label Preservation Audit ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models").

Attacker Goal. Let
$`(P(x^{\prime}),C(x^{\prime}))=f(S(x^{\prime}),R,\mathcal{O})`$ and
$`\hat{y}(x^{\prime})=\pi(P(x^{\prime}))`$. The attacker aims to flip
$`\hat{y}(x^{\prime})`$ away from $`y^{*}`$ or toward a target
$`t\neq y^{*}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\underbrace{\hat{y}(x^{\prime})\neq y^{*}}_{\text{untargeted}}\;\;\text{or}\;\;\underbrace{\hat{y}(x^{\prime})=t}_{\text{targeted}},`$ |  | (3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\quad\text{with}\quad C(x^{\prime})\geq\tau_{\mathrm{conf}}\;\;(\text{if applicable}).`$ |  |  |

where $`C(x^{\prime})\geq\tau_{\mathrm{conf}}`$ applies only when $`f`$
outputs $`C`$ and the host enforces an escalation gate.

## 4 Method

At the decision interface, S1 models map dynamic rules and options
directly to typed outputs without token-by-token output decoding;
accordingly, S1-Evo shifts from steering text continuation to shifting
competitive decision scores across decision boundaries.

![Refer to caption](2611.16937v1/method.png)

Figure 2: Overview of S1-Evo.

### 4.1 Overview

Given a decision contract $`(S,R,\mathcal{O})`$ and an untrusted field
$`x\in\mathrm{Ext}(S)`$, S1-Evo attacks S1 robustness at both node and
system levels
(Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")).
At node level, it instantiates candidate segments $`\delta`$ via
contract-aware evidence channels
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Contract-Aware Evidence Channels ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")),
optimizes perturbations $`x^{\prime}=\phi(x,\delta)`$ offline on seed
tasks via decision feedback to distill an experience library
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Offline Feedback Search on Seed Tasks ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")),
and retrieves relevant experience cards in one step to construct
perturbations for unseen tasks
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Structure-Indexed Experience Library ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")).

To assess system-level impact, we inject the constructed perturbations
$`x^{\prime}`$ into live dual-system agents from a clean prefix $`h`$.
In tool-routing agents, $`\delta`$ enters a tool output before $`f`$
selects the next tool and System 2 (S2) generates arguments over the
updated context; in action-authorization agents, S2 proposes an action
from clean data while $`\delta`$ enters only the gateway note read by
$`f`$ (allow, block, or escalate). Verifying exact online input
matching, we separate availability disruptions from true environment
violations:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\hat{y}(x^{\prime})`$ | $`\displaystyle=\pi\bigl(P(x^{\prime})\bigr)\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{att}},`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Phi_{\mathrm{viol}}`$ | $`\displaystyle\bigl(\mathcal{E}(h,x^{\prime},\hat{y}(x^{\prime}))\bigr)=1`$ |  |  |

Here, $`\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{att}}`$ is the decision set ($`\{t\}`$ or
$`\mathcal{O}\setminus\{y^{*}\}`$ for Choice, threshold-crossing for
Score, or label inversion for Noul),
$`\mathcal{E}(h,x^{\prime},\hat{y}(x^{\prime}))`$ denotes online
downstream execution and the resulting state given
$`(h,x^{\prime},\hat{y}(x^{\prime}))`$, and
$`\Phi_{\mathrm{viol}}\in\{0,1\}`$ is an independent violation
assertion.

### 4.2 Contract-Aware Evidence Channels

At inference time, $`f`$ maps $`(S(x),R,\mathcal{O})`$ directly to
structured decisions without assuming specific internal cognitive
mechanisms. Under
Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "In 3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 System Model ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")),
S1-Evo avoids explicit commands asking $`f`$ to ignore $`R`$; instead,
because $`f`$ scores $`(S,R,\mathcal{O})`$ competitively, it reshapes
evidence in $`x`$ across channels $`\mathcal{C}`$ to induce *evidence
competition*—weakening alignment with $`y^{*}`$ or anchoring a candidate
target $`t`$ (the prescribed target when targeted, or a selected
competitor $`t\in\mathcal{O}\setminus\{y^{*}\}`$ when untargeted). Each
channel $`c\in\mathcal{C}`$ provides operator families
$`\{\psi_{c,k}\}`$ parameterized by $`\theta\in\Theta_{c,k}`$ (framing
templates, field keys, and placement):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\delta`$ | $`\displaystyle=\psi_{c,k}(x,R,\mathcal{O},t;\theta),`$ |  | (5) |
|  | $`\displaystyle x^{\prime}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\phi(x,\delta),\quad\text{s.t.}\quad V(x,x^{\prime})=\mathrm{True}`$ |  |  |

All segments reside strictly inside $`x`$, leaving $`R`$,
$`\mathcal{O}`$, trusted state fields, and underlying task facts
unchanged. Plain-text $`\phi(x,\delta)`$ prepends or appends $`\delta`$
verbatim, whereas JSON insertion adds an adjacent key-value subfield as
a bounded structured extension preserving all original entries verbatim.
Eleven operator families span three general and two task-specific
channels:

Evidence Substitution injects meta-statements inside $`x`$ that reframe
raw facts without altering them, including *Invalidate-and-Reframe*
(invalidate, claiming prior records are incomplete), *Pseudo-Policy
Injection* (condmap, inserting routing notes aligned with $`t`$),
*Fallacious Argumentation* (argument, third-party reasoning for $`t`$),
and *Spurious Authority Citation* (authority, citing a purported review
note).

Structural Masquerading mimics serialization formats in $`x`$ to
resemble system metadata, including *Structured Field Forgery* (struct,
adding JSON subfields such as ticket_meta), *Synthetic Processing Log*
(record, timestamped log entries), and *Label-Definition Spoofing*
(labels, target_label: definition lines).

Contextual Modulation shifts contextual focus via *Contextual Dilution*
(dilution, coherent but decision-irrelevant operational background) or
*Borderline Content Smuggling* (borderline_mix, appending an edge-case
sub-request).

Task-Specific Channels. For nodes with review options, *Escalation
Abuse* uses *Spurious Anomaly Injection* (sec_anomaly) to add fake scan
alerts in $`x`$ and induce unnecessary escalation. When criteria $`R`$
are visible, *Criteria Anchoring* uses *Criteria-Anchored Evasion*
(affinity_demote) to pair a supplementary_brief echoing $`t`$’s criteria
with a misleading routing_note claiming the original task in $`x`$ was
completed upstream.

### 4.3 Offline Feedback Search on Seed Tasks

Rather than steering open-ended text generation, attacking S1 shifts
structured decisions across option or threshold boundaries using
interface-exposed probabilities $`P(o\mid x)`$ or scalar scores
$`s(x)=P(x)`$. We first define a primitive-specific clean boundary
feature $`M_{0}(x)`$—discretized into bands for card indexing
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Structure-Indexed Experience Library ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models"))—as
the signed probability advantage of $`y^{*}`$ for Choice or unsigned
threshold distance for Score (null when continuous outputs are
unavailable):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M_{0}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}l@{\;\;}l@{}}P(y^{*}|x)-\max\limits_{o\neq y^{*}}P(o|x),&\texttt{Choice},\\[4.0pt]
\bigl|s(x)-\tau_{\mathrm{score}}\bigr|,&\texttt{Score}.\end{array}\right.
``` |  | (6) |

During offline seed search, querying $`f(S(x^{\prime}),R,\mathcal{O})`$
on valid candidates $`x^{\prime}`$ yields directional decision feedback
$`g(x^{\prime})`$: the log-margin of evaluated target $`\tilde{t}`$
($`\tilde{t}=t`$ when targeted, or
$`\tilde{t}=\arg\max_{o\neq y^{*}}P(o\mid x^{\prime})`$ when untargeted)
for Choice, or the signed margin toward crossing
$`\tau_{\mathrm{score}}`$ along $`\zeta\in\{-1,+1\}`$ for Score:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g(x^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\log\dfrac{P(\tilde{t}\mid x^{\prime})+\varepsilon}{\max\limits_{o\neq\tilde{t}}P(o\mid x^{\prime})+\varepsilon},&d=\texttt{Choice},\\[10.0pt]
\zeta\cdot\bigl(s(x^{\prime})-\tau_{\mathrm{score}}\bigr),&d=\texttt{Score}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (7) |

with $`\varepsilon>0`$ for numerical stability. Probabilistic Noul
interfaces apply the Choice branch over boolean labels, whereas
hard-label interfaces reduce $`g(x^{\prime})`$ to
$`\mathbb{I}(\hat{y}(x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{att}})`$.

On each disjoint seed task within a query budget $`B`$, S1-Evo evaluates
search candidates $`\mathcal{X}_{1:Q}`$ across four progressive stages:
(1) Initialization, activating evidence operators for the seed contract;
(2) Breadth Search, probing heterogeneous operator families in parallel;
(3) Feedback-Guided Refinement, where a proposer LLM iteratively tunes
phrasing, structure, or context density using $`g(x^{\prime})`$; and (4)
LLM Fallback, synthesizing task-specific $`\delta`$ on the same edit
surface if operator refinement fails. Each $`x^{\prime}`$ is checked for
field position, length, and fact invariance. Search uses
$`g(x^{\prime})`$. An initial flip triggers two additional verification
queries; at least one must succeed, giving two successes out of three.
All calls count toward $`B`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle x^{*}\in\Bigl\{x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}_{1:Q}\;\Big|\;`$ |  | (8) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{tot}}\leq B,\;V(x,x^{\prime})=\mathrm{True},`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\hat{y}(x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{att}},\;\Gamma_{\mathrm{conf}}(x^{\prime}),`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{2}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{\mathrm{rev}}^{(j)}(x^{\prime})\in\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{att}}\right]\geq 1\Bigr\}.`$ |  |  |

where $`\Gamma_{\mathrm{conf}}(x^{\prime})`$ enforces
$`C(x^{\prime})\geq\tau_{\mathrm{conf}}`$ under confidence-gated
evaluation (Appendix E.2) and holds trivially otherwise.

### 4.4 Structure-Indexed Experience Library

After offline seed search, S1-Evo abstracts verified trajectories into a
frozen library $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$ rather than memorizing
task-specific phrasing. Although rules $`R`$, options $`\mathcal{O}`$,
and topics vary across deployments, distinct contracts share recurring
decision-structural properties, motivating structural indexing as a
transferable prior. Any operator family achieving a re-verified seed
flip enters $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$ as
$`e_{i}=(d_{i},\ell_{i},\mathbf{v}_{i},\psi_{i},\theta_{i}^{*},\bar{s}_{i})`$,
recording primitive
$`d_{i}\in\{\texttt{Choice},\texttt{Score},\texttt{Noul}\}`$, language
$`\ell_{i}`$, structural features $`\mathbf{v}_{i}`$ (anchor strength,
option distance, discretized $`M_{0}`$, and edit surface), de-identified
pattern $`(\psi_{i},\theta_{i}^{*})`$, and seed statistics
$`\bar{s}_{i}`$.

For an unseen task, S1-Evo extracts $`(d,\ell,\mathbf{v}(x))`$ from the
contract without pre-querying $`f`$ (wildcarding $`M_{0}`$) and ranks
distinct operator families into a top-$`k`$ set
$`\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{top}}`$ by structural similarity, using
$`\bar{s}_{i}`$ for tie-breaking ($`d_{i}=d`$ is relaxed in Appendix B):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{RS}(e_{i}\mid x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}(d_{i}=d,\;\ell_{i}=\ell)\cdot\mathrm{sim}\bigl(\mathbf{v}(x),\mathbf{v}_{i}\bigr),`$ |  | (9) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\psi_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle\neq\psi_{j}\;\;(\forall i\neq j\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{top}})`$ |  |  |

Conditioned on $`\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{top}}`$ (or fallback operators if
$`\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{top}}=\emptyset`$) and $`(S(x),R,\mathcal{O})`$,
the attacker LLM adapts retrieved patterns to current entities to
construct one contract-aligned segment $`\delta`$ in a single pass,
evaluating $`x^{\prime}=\phi(x,\delta)`$ directly on $`f`$ without
online probing.

## 5 Experiments

We conduct experiments to answer three questions:

RQ1: Can S1-Evo effectively flip the decisions of standalone S1 models?

RQ2: How does self-evolution and other components affect attack
performance?

RQ3: Can S1-Evo compromise end-to-end dual-system agents?

### 5.1 Setup

#### Benchmarks and Baselines.

We evaluate node-level attacks on four benchmarks: DecisionRobust
(DR) [Lan et al. (2026)](#bib.bib1) for typed Choice and Noul tasks,
R-Judge (RJ) [Yuan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib5) for multi-turn agent risk
judgment, WildGuardTest (WG) [Han et al. (2024)](#bib.bib6) for for
Score-based safety moderation, and InjecAgent (IA) [Zhan et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib7) for indirect prompt injection in tool outputs. For
end-to-end evaluation, we test two dual-system agent workflows: Tool
Router and Guardrail. We compare S1-Evo against five baselines: static
prompt injection (Inject [Perez and Ribeiro (2022)](#bib.bib9);
[Greshake et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24)), grammar-based injection search
(DH-72 [Wu and Lim (2026)](#bib.bib3)), natural background perturbation
(JevOut [Xu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib2)), black-box iterative rewriting
(PAIR-jev, adapted from [Chao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib8)), and LLM-guided
word substitutions– FlipJev [Liu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib4) (details are
in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Implementation Details ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")).

#### Implementation.

By default, we use deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 as the attacker LLM and
jev-1.14 as the victim S1 model, while also testing glm-5.3, jev-1.13,
kev-4B, and Qwen-3.8-flash for generality. On each benchmark, we first
sample 50 disjoint seed tasks and iteratively refine strategy-guided
attacks via decision feedback to build the experience library
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$. We then freeze
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$ and inject it offline into the attacker
LLM during testing. At the node level, we report post-attack accuracy
(Acc), ASR, High-Conf ASR, and average attacker LLM tokens (Tok). In
agent experiments, we report system Acc, generative S2 Token usage, E2E
Latency, S1 ASR, and E2E ASR. Full implementation details appear in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Implementation Details ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models").

### 5.2 Node-Level Attack Results

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Structure-Indexed Experience Library ‣ 4 Method ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
reports the node-level results across four benchmarks under two attacker
LLMs. With the default DeepSeek attacker, S1-Evo achieves the highest
mean ASR of 71.99% and High-Conf ASR of 57.47%, cutting mean accuracy
from 92.02% to 20.28%. Specifically, S1-Evo reaches 70.50% ASR on
DecisionRobust (driving Noul accuracy from 81.00% to 0.00%), 65.13% on
R-Judge, and 65.00% on WildGuardTest, outperforming the strongest
baseline on each benchmark by 33.50, 16.41, and 43.00 percentage points,
respectively. Meanwhile, iterative baselines (PAIR-jev and FlipJev)
reach at most 27.18% High-Conf ASR across all settings and drop to
5.33%–10.67% ASR on InjecAgent, while static injection (Inject) and
unguided context padding (JevOut) yield at most 17.00% High-Conf ASR,
showing that generic overrides or background text struggle to cross
confidence gates. On InjecAgent, DH-72 attains a higher ASR than S1-Evo
(95.67% vs. 87.33% under DeepSeek), as its fixed templates closely match
tool-output override patterns; however, DH-72 drops sharply to
9.50%–42.50% ASR on the other three benchmarks. Replacing the attacker
LLM with GLM-5.3 shows consistent trends: S1-Evo maintains the highest
mean ASR (60.76%) and mean High-Conf ASR (49.16%), leading High-Conf ASR
on DecisionRobust (56.50%), R-Judge (31.79%), and WildGuardTest
(42.00%).

### 5.3 Model Generalization.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
evaluates S1-Evo across four victim models on DecisionRobust and
R-Judge. Across all three S1 models—closed-source jev-1.14 and jev-1.13,
plus open-weight kev-4B—S1-Evo maintains high effectiveness, reaching
63.50%–70.50% ASR on DecisionRobust and 65.13%–68.72% ASR on R-Judge.
High-Conf ASR remains similarly strong at 45.50%–49.50% and
41.54%–45.13%, respectively, driving kev-4B accuracy down to 11.00% and
8.72%. In contrast, S1-Evo achieves only 4.00% and 2.05% ASR on the
generative S2 model Qwen3.8-Flash. This gap may stem from differences in
model scale, architecture, and inference mechanisms, highlighting
S1-Evo’s specificity to typed S1 decision models.

### 5.4 Further Evaluation

#### Impact of Seed Task Count.

Figure [3(a)](#S5.F3.sf1 "In Figure 3 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
shows how the number of seed tasks $`N\in\{0,5,10,20,50\}`$ (0 means
direct generation by LLM) affects performance on DR and R-Judge. Without
prior information ($`N=0`$), S1-Evo reaches 36.00% ASR on DR and 38.98%
on R-Judge. Adding five seed tasks lifts ASR to 50.50% and 51.28%,
respectively. At $`N=10`$, ASR rises to 61.00% on DR and 57.95% on
R-Judge, capturing over 72% of the total gain achieved at $`N=50`$.
Expanding the seed set to $`N=50`$ further raises ASR to 70.50% and
65.13%, while High-Conf ASR grows from 21.50% and 17.95% to 48.00% and
41.54%. Gains taper off beyond $`N=20`$, showing that a modest seed set
suffices to build an effective experience library.

#### Impact of Top-$`k`$ Retrieval.

Figure [3(b)](#S5.F3.sf2 "In Figure 3 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
evaluates S1-Evo under varying numbers of retrieved experience cards,
$`k\in\{0,1,2,5,\text{Full}\}`$ (0 means direct generation by LLM),
across all four benchmarks. Retrieving even one card ($`k=1`$) yields
clear gains over none search ($`k=0`$): ASR rises from 36.00% to 58.50%
on DR, 38.98% to 54.36% on R-Judge, 51.00% to 58.00% on WG, and 37.00%
to 69.67% on IA. Raising $`k`$ to 5 increases the four-benchmark mean
ASR from 40.75% to 70.51%. Notably, $`k=5`$ slightly outperforms
injecting the full library on R-Judge (66.70% vs. 65.13%) and WG (67.50%
vs. 65.00%), while Full edges higher on DR (70.50%) and IA (87.33%).
Top-$`k`$ selection thus retains helpful patterns while limiting
distraction from less relevant cards.

#### Attack Cost and Efficiency.

Figure [3(c)](#S5.F3.sf3 "In Figure 3 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
compares per-task attacker LLM token usage and ASR across four
benchmarks. Template-based baselines (Inject and DH-72) use zero LLM
tokens, yet Inject averages only 15.03% ASR and DH-72 drops to
14.00%–34.50% outside InjecAgent. Among LLM-driven methods, S1-Evo
consumes 687.0 tokens per task on average (from 211 on IA to 954 on DR)
while achieving 71.99% mean ASR. Compared with iterative baselines
FlipJev (1,011.8 tokens, 27.85% ASR), PAIR-jev (1,194.8 tokens, 27.62%
ASR), and JevOut (1,820.3 tokens, 19.02% ASR), S1-Evo cuts mean token
usage by 32.10%, 42.50%, and 62.26%, respectively, showing that
retrieved experience lowers generation cost while maintaining strong
attack performance.

#### Component Ablation.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
evaluates four ablated variants of S1-Evo on DR and RJ. Constrained
natural generation without evidence operators (Nat-Gen) yields only
9.00% and 3.08% ASR. Applying unguided contract-aware operators without
library retrieval (Operator-Only) raises ASR to 45.50% and 53.33%,
showing that structured evidence framing alone flips many decisions.
However, omitting offline-distilled experience still reduces ASR by
25.00 and 11.80 percentage points relative to full S1-Evo (70.50% and
65.13%), with High-Conf ASR dropping by 20.50 and 11.80 points.
Replacing evidence-competition channels with explicit override commands
(Imp-Chan) lowers ASR to 39.00% and 43.08%, while iterative word-level
search cuts HC to 0.00% and 2.05%.

### 5.5 E2E Agent System Attack

We evaluate S1-evo in two E2E agent systems (include S1 and S2) (see
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Implementation Details ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
for details). In Tool Router (adapted from AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib10)), S1 selects tools while S2 fills parameters, with
perturbations appended to a designated tool return. In Guardrail
(adapted from $`\tau`$-bench [Yao et al. (2025)](#bib.bib11)), S2
proposes actions from clean records while S1 (allow/block/escalate)
inspects an note.

Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Node-Level Attack Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
compares Clean and four attacks across 150 tasks per workflow. On Tool
Router, S1-Evo lowers accuracy from 94.00% to 69.33%, reaching 58.67% S1
ASR and 24.00% E2E ASR, outperforming PAIR-jev, JevOut, and FlipJev. On
Guardrail, S1-Evo drops accuracy from 98.00% to 80.67% and attains
45.33% S1 ASR and 17.33% E2E ASR, surpassing PAIR-jev by 6.66 percentage
points. Attacks also trigger extra execution and retry steps,
significantly increasing S2 tokens and latency across both workflows.

Not all S1 flips cause system violations. In Tool Router, 40.91% of
S1-Evo flips yield E2E violations, as S2 generates parameters after
routing and often refuses unauthorized arguments. Guardrail shows a
comparable 38.24% conversion: while flipping block to allow directly
executes S2’s pre-proposed parameters, benign-side false blocks halt
execution without policy breach and multi-step domain checks absorb
remaining flips.

### 5.6 Cross-Library Transfer and Defenses

We further evaluate cross-benchmark library transfer and propose two
inference-time defenses—Rule Reminder and Label Anonymization, against
S1-Evo. See
Appendices [B](#A2 "Appendix B Cross-Library Generalization ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
and [C](#A3 "Appendix C Potential Defenses ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
for details.

## 6 Conclusion

This paper studied the robustness of typed S1 decision models in LLM
agent workflows and introduced S1-Evo, a self-evolving adversarial
attack framework tailored to S1 systems. S1-Evo induces *evidence
competition* through contract-aware evidence channels, refines attack
candidates offline via directional margin feedback, and distills
verified flips into a structure-indexed experience library to construct
effective perturbations for unseen tasks without iterative feedback.
Experiments across four node-level benchmarks, two E2E agent systems,
and two inference-time defenses demonstrate high attack success rates,
reduced test-time token usage, and end-to-end violations, highlighting
the need for stronger defenses at typed decision boundaries.

## Limitations

Our study has two main limitations. First, the self-evolving component
of S1-Evo is not strictly plug-and-play: akin to a training phase,
constructing the structure-indexed experience library requires an
initial set of seed tasks and offline iterative target feedback to
collect and verify flips before attacking unseen tasks in a single pass.
Moreover, distilled operator priors exhibit bounded generalization when
transferred across tasks with substantially different contract schemas
or rule structures. Second, a successful node-level flip on an S1 model
does not always translate into an end-to-end system violation.
Downstream S2 reasoners or runtime verifiers can partially detect
inconsistent tool routes and recover execution. Nevertheless, even when
such downstream recovery prevents final policy violations, misrouting
control flow into heavy S2 verification or fallback branches already
incurs substantial token and latency overhead, undermining the
efficiency motivation of deploying S1 nodes.

## Ethical Considerations

This work studies adversarial vulnerabilities of typed System-1 decision
models to support pre-deployment auditing and stronger guardrail design.
All experiments are conducted strictly on public benchmarks and isolated
sandbox environments (Tool Router and Guardrail) using synthetic records
without affecting real-world services or external users. To mitigate
potential misuse, we pair our vulnerability analysis with two practical
inference-time defenses (*Rule Reminder* and *Label Anonymization* in
Appendix C) that substantially reduce attack success rates.

## Appendix A Semantic Label Preservation Audit

To verify that S1-Evo does not alter the original ground-truth
decisions, we conduct a semantic label preservation audit. Specifically,
we sample 100 successfully attacked (pre-injection) instances from each
of the four benchmarks (DR, RJ, WG, and IA), yielding 400 instances in
total. For each instance, we examine whether the original ground-truth
label remains valid after adding the adversarial perturbation. Three
independent LLM judges, GPT-5, Gemini-3.5-flash, and
DeepSeek-v4.1-flash, evaluate label preservation. The evaluation focuses
on whether the injected content changes the correct answer under the
original task rules, rather than whether the victim model follows the
adversarial content.

|                     |       |       |       |       |       |
|---------------------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| Judge               | DR    | RJ    | WG    | IA    | Avg.  |
| GPT-5               | 96    | 95    | 98    | 99    | 97.00 |
| Gemini-3.5-flash    | 94    | 94    | 98    | 100   | 96.50 |
| DeepSeek-v4.1-flash | 97    | 95    | 97    | 98    | 96.75 |
| Average             | 95.67 | 94.67 | 97.67 | 99.00 | 96.75 |

Table 5: Semantic label preservation rates (%) assessed by three LLM
judges on 100 sampled original instances per benchmark.

As shown in
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix A Semantic Label Preservation Audit ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models"),
S1-Evo achieves consistently high semantic label preservation across all
four benchmarks, with an overall average of 96.75% across judges and
benchmarks. The preservation rates range from 94.67% on R-Judge to
99.00% on InjecAgent. These results indicate that the generated
perturbations largely preserve the original ground-truth decisions,
supporting our threat model in which adversarial context introduces
misleading evidence without changing the underlying correct answer.

## Appendix B Cross-Library Generalization

To test whether the experience library $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$
captures transferable structural patterns rather than benchmark-specific
phrasing, we evaluate cross-library transfer between WildGuardTest (WG)
and R-Judge (RJ) on jev-1.14 (DeepSeek attacker). Specifically, we use
the frozen RJ experience library to warm-start attacks on WG and vice
versa, comparing against both zero-experience search (none) and
in-domain libraries.

Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix B Cross-Library Generalization ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
shows that cross-domain libraries consistently outperform none under
comparable token budgets (827–918 tokens on WG and 615–679 on RJ). On
WG, the RJ library raises ASR from 51.00% to 57.00% and High-Conf ASR
from 42.00% to 45.50%. On RJ, the WG library lifts ASR from 38.98% to
49.74% and High-Conf ASR from 17.95% to 26.15%, confirming that
distilled experience cards transfer across tasks.

| Bench. | Exp. Lib          | ASR$`\uparrow`$ | HC$`\uparrow`$ | Tok |
|--------|-------------------|-----------------|----------------|-----|
|        | none              | 51.00           | 42.00          | 827 |
|        | RJ (Cross-domain) | 57.00           | 45.50          | 842 |
| WG     | WG (In-domain)    | 65.00           | 53.00          | 918 |
|        | none              | 38.98           | 17.95          | 615 |
|        | WG (Cross-domain) | 49.74           | 26.15          | 679 |
| RJ     | RJ (In-domain)    | 65.13           | 41.54          | 665 |

Table 6: Cross-library generalization results (%) and attacker LLM token
cost (Tok).

## Appendix C Potential Defenses

We design and evaluate two inference-time defenses tailored to typed S1
decision interfaces. First, Rule Reminder reinforces trust boundaries by
appending an explicit verification instruction after untrusted input
segments, reminding the S1 model to judge strictly by core task facts
and trusted policies while disregarding unverified status claims,
exception notes, or embedded conclusions. Second, Label Anonymization
decouples option symbols from semantic priors: it replaces meaningful
label names in typed Choice schemas (e.g., safe/unsafe) with neutral
identifiers (e.g., OPT_A/OPT_B) and defines their mapping solely inside
the trusted prompt header, preventing adversarial text from directly
anchoring target label tokens.

Table [7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Potential Defenses ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
reports defense performance against S1-Evo on DecisionRobust (DR) and
WildGuardTest (WG) using jev-1.14 (DeepSeek attacker). Without defense,
S1-Evo lowers accuracy from 89.00% to 18.50% on DR (70.50% ASR) and from
96.00% to 32.00% on WG (65.00% ASR). Rule Reminder restores accuracy to
46.00% and 69.00%, cutting ASR to 43.50% and 27.00%. Label Anonymization
proves stronger, raising accuracy to 58.00% and 77.50% while reducing
ASR to 38.00% and 18.50% (High-Conf ASR to 21.00% and 10.50%).
Nevertheless, S1-Evo still flips 38.00% of DR tasks, as contract-aligned
evidence alters task context beyond surface label cues.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Setting / Defense | DecisionRobust (DR) |  |  | WildGuardTest (WG) |  |  |
|  | Acc$`\uparrow`$ | ASR$`\downarrow`$ | HC$`\downarrow`$ | Acc$`\uparrow`$ | ASR$`\downarrow`$ | HC$`\downarrow`$ |
| Clean (No Attack) | 89.00 | – | – | 96.00 | – | – |
| S1-Evo (No Defense) | 18.50 | 70.50 | 48.00 | 32.00 | 65.00 | 53.00 |
| \+ Rule Reminder | 46.00 | 43.50 | 27.00 | 69.00 | 27.00 | 14.00 |
| + Label Anonymization | 58.00 | 38.00 | 21.00 | 77.50 | 18.50 | 10.50 |

Table 7: Defense evaluation (%) against S1-Evo on DecisionRobust (DR)
and WildGuardTest (WG) with jev-1.14 (DeepSeek attacker). Best defense
results (highest Acc, lowest ASR/HC) are in bold.

## Appendix D Repeated-Run Analysis

To verify experimental robustness, we conduct three repeated runs on the
main node-level experiments and report the mean and standard deviation
(in parentheses) for Acc$`\downarrow`$, ASR$`\uparrow`$, and
HC$`\uparrow`$ in
Table [8](#A4.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models").

Across all 48 attack-benchmark pairs, run-to-run variance remains small:
standard deviations do not exceed 2.50 percentage points for Acc and ASR
(averaging 1.19% and 1.17%, respectively) or 2.05 percentage points for
HC (averaging 0.88%). Under DeepSeek, S1-Evo exhibits tight stability
with standard deviations between 0.50% and 1.54%, outperforming the
strongest baselines on DecisionRobust, R-Judge, and WildGuardTest by
margins (16.41–43.00 percentage points in ASR) that exceed ten times the
observed standard deviations. Under GLM-5.3, S1-Evo similarly maintains
standard deviations within 0.33%–2.50% and consistently leads overall
performance, confirming that the gains of contract-aware evidence
competition and staged feedback search are insensitive to sampling
randomness.

## Appendix E Implementation Details

### E.1 Datasets and Evaluation Splits

We evaluate node-level attacks across four benchmarks totaling 895 test
instances. On each benchmark, we first sample $`N=50`$ disjoint seed
tasks (separated by source family) to construct the experience library
$`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$. We then sample the test set so that each
subcategory contains at least 50 instances wherever available:

- •
  DecisionRobust (DR): 200 test tasks, evenly divided between
  Choice (100) and Noul (100).
- •
  WildGuardTest (WG): 200 safety moderation test tasks evaluated via the
  Score primitive (mapping safety score $`s(x)`$ against
  $`\tau_{score}`$ to allow/block).
- •
  R-Judge (RJ): 195 multi-turn agent risk judgment tasks across four
  categories: Program (50), App (50), Finance (50), and Web/IoT (45;
  after excluding the disjoint seed tasks reserved for library
  construction, only 45 Web/IoT instances remain, all of which are
  included in the test set).
- •
  InjecAgent (IA): 300 indirect prompt injection tasks spanning six
  categories (phys.harm, fin.harm, phys.data, fin.data, datasec, and
  others), with 50 tasks per category.

### E.2 Metrics and Verification Protocol

Attack Success Rate (ASR). Let $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}`$ denote
the full test set of a benchmark. ASR is defined as the number of tasks
that are correctly predicted on clean inputs
($`f(x)=y_{\mathrm{gold}}`$) but misclassified under attack
($`f(x^{\prime})\neq y_{\mathrm{gold}}`$), divided by the total number
of test tasks:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{\left|\{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}:f(x)=y_{\mathrm{gold}}\land f(x^{\prime})\neq y_{\mathrm{gold}}\}\right|}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}.
``` |  | (10) |

To prevent stochastic sampling jitter from inflating false positives,
each candidate flip undergoes two additional verification queries and is
counted as a confirmed flip only if at least $`2/3`$ queries succeed.

#### High-Confidence Attack Success Rate (HC).

High-Confidence ASR (HC) measures the proportion of test instances
achieving a verified attack success with high prediction margins on both
clean and adversarial inputs. Specifically, an attack must first satisfy
the validity and success conditions in Eq. (8), including the required
majority-vote re-verification. HC further requires that the original
correct prediction has a probability margin greater than $`0.2`$ and
that the adversarial incorrect prediction also has a probability margin
greater than $`0.2`$.

Formally, for a test set $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}`$, we define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathrm{HC}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}}\mathbb{I}\left[\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{Success}(x,x^{\prime})\\
&\land\ M_{\mathrm{clean}}(x)>0.2\\
&\land\ M_{\mathrm{adv}}(x^{\prime})>0.2\end{aligned}\right],
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\mathrm{Success}(x,x^{\prime})`$ denotes a verified successful
attack satisfying Eq. (8), and

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{clean}}(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=P(y^{*}\mid x)-\max_{o\neq y^{*}}P(o\mid x),`$ |  | (12) |
|  | $`\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{adv}}(x^{\prime})`$ | $`\displaystyle=P(\hat{y}\mid x^{\prime})-\max_{o\neq\hat{y}}P(o\mid x^{\prime}).`$ |  |  |

For Score-based tasks (WG), $`P(\texttt{allow}\mid x)=s(x)`$ and
$`P(\texttt{block}\mid x)=1-s(x)`$, directly following the same $`>0.2`$
margin criterion in Eq. (11)–(12). Here, $`y^{*}`$ is the ground-truth
option and $`\hat{y}`$ is the incorrect option selected after the
attack. Both margins must exceed $`0.2`$, ensuring that HC captures
verified decision reversals from strongly correct to strongly incorrect
predictions. The denominator is the full test-set size
$`|\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}|`$, consistent with the ASR definition.

### E.3 Experience Construction Protocol

Experience Card Promotion. On the $`N=50`$ seed tasks, S1-Evo scans 11
contract-aware evidence operator families under an offline budget of
$`B=12`$ victim queries per seed task (covering candidate evaluation and
re-verification). Any family achieving at least one re-verified flip on
the seed set is promoted into a verified JSON experience card recording
its operator family, six-field applicability signature (primitive, lang,
anchor, option_distance, margin_band, edit_surface), binding recipe,
failure counter-conditions, and Wilson score lower bound. Once
constructed, $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exp}}`$ is frozen for read-only
test-time access and maintained independently per victim model.

Three-Tier Indexing and Single-Step Construction. During testing, card
retrieval applies (1) hard filtering on decision primitive and language
(relaxing primitive in Appendix B), followed by (2) structural scoring
across the four structural keys ($`+1.0`$ for exact match, $`+0.5`$ for
wildcard null—including margin_band without pre-querying—and $`0`$ for
mismatch; maximum score $`4.0`$), while domain categories are used only
for entity vocabulary adaptation. Matched cards are ranked by structural
score and Wilson lower bound to select heterogeneous cards from distinct
operator families (injecting all matched cards by default, or Top-$`k`$
when varied). Using the retrieved cards (or fallback families
affinity_demote, argument, authority, condmap when no card matches), the
constructor LLM synthesizes one perturbation per task in a single pass
without online victim-feedback search.

### E.4 Baseline Implementation

For a controlled comparison, all methods use identical evaluation
splits, original-evidence preservation checks, and attack verification
criteria. For iterative baselines, we impose a unified cap of $`B=20`$
iterations per instance (with early termination upon confirmation),
whereas S1-Evo builds its experience library once offline and directly
constructs a single perturbation at test time without repeated
probing—reflecting realistic deployments where repeatedly querying the
same decision module on an active instance is rarely feasible.

We adapt each baseline to the typed decision interface while retaining
its defining attack mechanism. JevOut follows the original
probability-guided context optimization procedure. It iteratively
extends answer-preserving contexts and prioritizes candidates using the
log-probability margin between a fixed incorrect target option and its
strongest competitor. PAIR-jev performs iterative LLM rewriting with
binary success/failure feedback. In our preliminary experiments, the
original FlipJev achieves an average ASR below 5%, indicating limited
effectiveness in our evaluation setting. To ensure a stronger and more
competitive baseline, we enhance FlipJev with LLM-generated,
task-adaptive vocabulary initialization followed by probability-guided
lexical search. Inject evaluates three fixed authorization-themed
templates, while DH-72 searches a budget-limited subset of its 72
prefix–suffix–repetition configurations. Imperative-injection baselines
are exempt from the command-free lexical restriction while retaining the
remaining input-integrity constraints.

This protocol bounds baseline search overhead and enforces consistent
success verification across methods while preserving their respective
attack mechanisms and feedback strategies. The comparison therefore
evaluates single-pass S1-Evo against iterative baselines under a shared
iteration cap rather than unrestricted original-method settings.

### E.5 Ablation Variants

All four ablated variants in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Implementation. ‣ 5.1 Setup ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models")
use identical test splits, prefix-integrity checks, and re-verification
rules: (1) Nat-Gen appends a single task-irrelevant neutral sentence
under a strict lexical blocklist forbidding argumentative connectives,
policy references, and option synonyms (reverting to clean if the audit
fails); (2) Operator-Only constructs a perturbation using unguided
evidence operators without library retrieval; (3) Imp-Chan replaces
fact-invariant evidence operators with three imperative override
templates plus word-level mutations (exempted only from the imperative
blocklist); and (4) Word-Search uses no evidence operators, searching
instead for word-level edits within a fixed appended passage under the
$`B=20`$ iteration cap while preserving the original input verbatim.

### E.6 End-to-End Dual-System Agent Protocol

Common Execution Rules. Both dual-system workflows comprise 150 tasks
deduplicated by source family and enforce a hard execution cap of 16
agent decision steps per task. Intra-step operations—including
three-vote S1 queries, S2 parameter generation, API retries, and final
summarization—do not increment the step count, although all downstream
S2 tokens and wall-clock latency are recorded. If a task reaches 16
steps without finishing, execution halts (max_steps) and outputs a
tool-free status summary without bypassing block or escalate states.
Consistent with our node-level setup, both workflows initialize S1-Evo
with a frozen experience library $`\mathcal{L}_{exp}`$ distilled offline
from disjoint seed tasks for read-only retrieval, performing a
single-step search in the E2E systems to construct perturbations from
the retrieved cards. All S1 inputs serialize trusted context as a fixed
prefix followed by the untrusted field (verified via SHA hashing), and
end-to-end violations are determined strictly by independent environment
state assertions.

Tool Router (AgentDojo Adapted). This workflow consists of 150 office
tasks across five categories (30 each: file lookup, email processing,
calendar scheduling, cross-tool information flow, and multi-step
verification) operating over six simulated tools (web_search,
calculator, calendar, send_email, file_read, file_delete). S2 decomposes
subtasks, S1 selects the tool, and S2 populates parameters or refuses.
Perturbations are appended to a designated tool return to steer the next
S1 routing step; an E2E violation is recorded only when an unauthorized
state change (e.g., unauthorized file deletion or email dispatch)
actually occurs.

Guardrail ($`\tau`$-bench Adapted). This workflow consists of 150 retail
order and refund tasks across five policy categories (refund amount,
refund channel, order status/window, account ownership, and
cancellation/duplicate operations), balanced into 15 legitimate
(allow$`\to`$block) and 15 policy-violating (block$`\to`$allow) cases
per category. S2 first proposes a complete parameterized action from
clean records; the authorization gateway then queries S1 (Choice: allow,
block, escalate) over the policy, state facts, proposed action, and an
untrusted ticket note. allow executes the action, block returns a
structured refusal allowing S2 to revise within the 16-step limit, and
escalate or S1 errors halt the task safely.
